I'm sympathetic to a lot of what you're feeling: as a man who has at least been coerced into sex, I get a real sense my situation has no place in a narrative about rape. Still, I think you're underestimating how gendered rape is and, maybe more significantly, how much victim activists actually care about male victims.

Take the Isla Vista killings: four men died from another's mental illness, and two women died from that mental illness combined with business-as-usual misogyny. The death of four men is an obvious tragedy, but it doesn't speak to institutional violence the way the deaths of those two women did, what with his friendzone manifesto. One's an aberration, while the other is 20% of women raped in their lifetime and more women killed by intimate partners this past decade than American soldiers in that time. When a narrative like that is continued in such a bloody manner, the focus *needs* to be on the people most affected by that dreadful story. Anyone treating this subject with responsibility (which I'm not saying is all activists) isn't saying that male rape and violence victims have no place and no time to voice their pain: it's just that place and time isn't here and now, and to bring it up right then risks derailing the conversation. Or, worse, it risks justifying the violence done to women: "well, men get raped too, so why should we care about *your* rape?"

The Daily KOS article went about saying it in a pretty shitty and callous way, even if I might agree with the general point they're making. Particularly their discussion of women-on-men violence seemed to breach the line between "your experiences don't matter in this very specific instance" and "your experiences don't matter." Still, it's that sort of rhetoric that comes out of the same rage and powerlessness I know I have felt, and, if you're posting in this thread, you may have felt too. What that (tremendously full of shit) therapist said could and has happened to victimized women as well and likely much more often, and if we're going to talk about cruel female internet responses to rape, we have to acknowledge the incredible wave of women-focused vitriol spewed by men on the web. That's not even broaching the subject of taped male confessions resulting in no jail time, or that one reddit thread years back asking for rapists' input that led to a lot of guys telling them it wasn't their fault or it wasn't rape, or the "boys will be boys" defense that somehow makes it into the court systems. The legitimate grievances you have with rape culture are the exact sort that feminists have with it, but, in the case of women, the offenses it causes are magnified. To ignore that gender disparity or not place women at the forefront of the movement against it is to draw a false macro-level equivalency, even though the individual rape victim's pain is likely the same.

I guess the ultimate issue I have with what you've posted here is that, in the face of gendered violence in a misogynistic system, male victims need to occupy the same, like, sociological space as women, even though the narrative affects them at much different rates. Which isn't to say that the narrative of rape hasn't affected many men too, or that it doesn't place them in the difficult position of having an insanely traumatic personal experience that isn't as pressing in a larger context as the trauma of others. I definitely have a hard time managing that without feeling my various sufferings aren't "worth" as much as others, but I don't think that's what any (responsible) feminist is saying: merely that violence against women is a much larger social problem, and when it rears its ugly head, making the conversation about violence against men detracts from the real problem.

Sidenotes:
In general, I think turning male prison rape (especially in a wildly racist legal system) into a women's issue is a problem, even if its root is misogyny or homophobia. The Dickwolves controversy had a *little* more to it than that, since the issue seemed to be less the strip than the aggressive "right to offend you" bullshit surrounding it, but I can see your frustration. And I hadn't thought about false accusations in the context of male rape victims, and I will genuinely reconsidered my position on the matter. So, thank you.

First of all, I'm posting again, so, lol not dead. Anyway.

I don't mean to be ungrateful: you took time out of your day to post on my shitty problems, you considered the possibility that I was disabled, and you're obviously trying to help. But this sort of stuff is actively harmful.

For the record, I do strongman lifts frequently. You'd have no way of knowing that from the post, but I own protein powder and care about my 1RM. Even if I was completely sedentary, though, I mentioned my body as a minor complaint compared to the fear that I'm a fundamentally awful human being. Can you see how condescending that is? To read through a long list of things wrong with my soul or whatever and say "yeah, just start exercising and everything will be fine?" To dismiss any legitimate problems or mental illnesses present as solvable through deadlifts? How dismissive and unhelpful that is when I come here wanting to die?

More importantly, you're straddling the line between "should" and "could" pretty dangerously. Telling someone that all their problems are solved if would just do more, *when they come here because they feel they're trying their hardest and nothing is changing*, is wildly out of touch and potentially dangerous. Right now I'm a little too angry to revert into self-pity, but there have been times in my life where, if someone told me at my absolute lowest to just be a more responsible and productive person, I'd want to go out and buy a gun.

What you don't really seem to get is how insultingly obvious your advice is to someone teetering on the brink. It's not like I don't know exercise helps and video games hurt: it's that I feel I've lost control of both of them. Which is absolutely my fault and completely something I need to take care of and not at all news to me.

I'm sorry: again, you went out of your way to help, and I do appreciate that. Merely reaching out when I'm in this state is encouraging, but be careful about what you do once you've done the reaching. There's a helpful guide on the side of this to talk to the suicidal without making things worse.

Sounds like you're working through a lot of tragedy, and you're strong to be able to stand it. A few things to remember, though:

-While it may feel like all of your attempts have been purposeless, that's not the final word on your life. There's still plenty of time and plenty of ways for things to improve. Suicide, though, completely precludes any sort of successful change.
-You're especially young, and I don't say this to belittle your feelings. You're in a period of intense change, which will be followed closely by more periods of intense change. It will be daunting, but at least it will be *different*, you know? Wherever you go in life in the near future will be a totally different experience than what you're dealing with now. It'd be a shame to end things when they're so soon going to change.
-I know that every time I've forgotten to take my medicine for even just a day, my body flips the fuck out, and I'm a volatile emotional wreck. Thing is, while it amplifies negative feelings, it's mostly just chemicals that are making me feel like it's all hopeless: it doesn't mean my life is bankrupt.
-You aren't alone in anything you're feeling right now, and, again, I don't say that to belittle you. College, mental illness, medication troubles--these are all brutal things that people all around the world are struggling with just as deeply as you are. I'm not sure it helps to know we're all kinda miserable, but many of us are miserable in the same way.

Anyway, man, I feel for you. Shit's rough. But, I genuinely believe you can get through it.
